# Applying a lower-dimensional theorem to actual affine slices

This records the contributor's direct prelimit alternative to reconstructing a
convex lift of a singular rate law. It is conditional only on having
already proved the desired center theorem in LOWER continuous
dimension. It is not an invocation of OC in the dimension currently
under study, and it gives no critical-cap incidence payment.

## 1. Exact affine chart and measure

Let d>=1 and let D be a compact convex set in R^n x R^d. In the
application D is ONE actual global active cell

    C intersect intersection_l {A_i<=A_l}.

Let A(z,x)=a+b dot z+c dot x be affine with c!=0, and fix a real
level s. Consider its actual mixed affine slice

    T=D intersect {A=s} intersect (Z^n x R^d).

Write N=d-1. Choose an isometry E:R^N -> c-perpendicular and set

    x_s(z)=[(s-a-b dot z)/|c|^2]c,
    F(z,y)=(z,x_s(z)+Ey).                              (1)

This is an affine bijection from R^n x R^N onto {A=s}; it leaves the
integer base unchanged. On each fixed base its continuous part is
an isometry. Thus, with D'=F inverse of D intersect {A=s},

    sum_z H_N(T_z)=sum_z vol_N(D'_z),                   (2)

including N=0 with counting measure. The common inverse-coarea
factor 1/(M lambda |c|), when present, multiplies every fiber
equally and cancels from every normalized depth.

Every ambient affine halfspace pulls back by F to an affine
halfspace in the chart, unless its restricted functional is constant.
A constant restriction is either the whole chart or empty; a cap
containing a selected point is the former. Conversely, every chart
halfspace extends to an ambient halfspace by extending its affine
functional from the affine plane {A=s}. Therefore normalized
halfspace depth is preserved exactly in both directions.

## 2. Ambient dimension and boundary fibers

Assume the total measure in (2) is positive. Let P_s be ALL integer
bases with a nonempty slice D'_z, including lower-dimensional ones.
It is finite. Replace D' by the canonical sampled hull

    K=conv union_(z in P_s) ({z} x D'_z).                (3)

Its sampled fibers are exactly D'_z. One inclusion is immediate.
For the other, convexity of D' puts every anchored combination of
sampled points back in its actual target section. The projection
of K is B=conv(P_s), and

    P_s=B intersect Z^n.

Indeed every integer base of B has a convex combination of sampled
points above it, hence a nonempty actual section.

At least one sampled fiber has positive N-volume. If N>=1 this
fiber is an N-dimensional convex body. If N=0 it is a singleton,
the full zero-dimensional body. Put k=dim B. The affine dimension
of K is k+N: one fiber supplies N independent vertical directions,
and the projected bases supply the remaining k independent
directions. Hence K is full dimensional in its relative space.

Use a basis of the saturated lattice span(B-B) intersect Z^n and
translate by an integer base point. This identifies the relative
space with R^k x R^N and its sampled bases with Z^k. The continuous
N-dimensional fiber measure is unchanged. All original nonempty
boundary fibers remain present. They carry zero N-volume when
N>=1 and their dimension is smaller, but they are not deleted
from the convex body or from possible selected points.

Thus (3) is a legitimate convex body for a theorem in dimensions
(k,N). No full dimensionality of every integer fiber, interior
real-base projection point, or general position assumption is
needed.

## 3. The legitimate inductive consequence

Suppose OC has ALREADY been established for arbitrary integer
dimension and continuous dimension N=d-1. Apply it to K. Since
its mixed intersection has Hausdorff dimension N and positive
measure, it supplies one point (z,y) in its actual sampled set
with every chart containing halfspace carrying at least

    2^(-k) Gamma_N sum_z vol_N(D'_z).                   (4)

The point F(z,y) belongs to the original slice T itself, and all
closed ambient halfspaces through it satisfy the same inequality
by Sections 1--2. In particular the weaker factor 2^(-n) Gamma_N
holds. For N=0, Gamma_0=1 and the required input is the already
classical pure-integer center theorem. If k=N=0, T is one point
and the conclusion is immediate without invoking a theorem whose
ambient dimension must be positive.

If the measure in (2) is zero, this statement yields no positive
inverse-coarea mass and the corresponding rate component is
irrelevant to this N-volume application. One may separately apply
an intrinsic theorem to a lower-dimensional nonempty slice, but
its measure would not be the coarea density in (2).

If c=0, the slice equation restricts only the integer base and does
not lower the continuous dimension. That case is expressly outside
this argument; it cannot be disguised as d-1 induction.

## 4. What remains after applying this before the limit

This use of induction takes place on the ACTUAL prelimit body and
actual prelimit halfspaces. No radial reconstruction, guessed
conditional log-concavity, or replacement of selected boundary
fractions by closed-halfspace mass is needed to justify (4).

It does not show that the selected slice point has a prescribed
source base, belongs to the finite actual deepest mark set, or
is captured by a given fraction of the ORIGINAL critical-cap law.
Those caps were selected at other source marks. The assertion
that a cap contains a slice center is still a separate geometric
condition.

When passing to a singular limit, jointly retain the selected
points and actual cap-incidence records. A limiting cap may have
positive mass on its boundary, even when every prelimit slice
cap boundary was null. The limit of selected fractions is then
not automatically the mass of the limiting closed halfspace.
This issue persists even after a common affine blow-up whenever
the limiting continuous normal is zero on a sampled fiber.
Equation (4) remains correct before the limit; it supplies no
unproved identification of these different boundary quantities.
